task.goal: Create a way to reduce peak-hour waiting at a small bakery without adding staff or making rushed orders more error-prone.
hard_constraints: Two staff handle counter, packing and payment in a 90-minute peak.
No paid kiosk, app requirement or advance customer data collection.
Observe queue time and order errors against the present single line.
task.available_resources: Paper signs, tickets and one week of aggregate hourly counts.
task.expected_result: A workable service mechanism and small test.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A two-person relay with one visible order ticket
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace both staff switching among counter, packing and payment with a temporary division of work during the 90-minute peak. One person takes orders and payments; the other packs. Customers remain in one ordering line, then wait beside the collection point with a numbered paper ticket. The matching ticket travels with the order. The packer checks the contents against that ticket before calling the number; unclear orders return to the counter person for clarification rather than being guessed.

The mechanism is overlapping payment and packing while reducing repeated task switching. Moving customers out of the ordering line alone is not a benefit: success means less time from joining the line to receiving a correct order. Keep only two paid orders awaiting packing initially. When that limit is reached, the counter person pauses new orders and helps finish the oldest one, preventing an invisible packing backlog.

This assumes the counter has room for a small collection area, payment and packing can physically overlap, and neither activity overwhelmingly dominates service time. It also assumes existing paper can record orders legibly without creating excessive writing work. Mixed or unusual orders may erase the benefit. Implementation needs numbered paper slips, a collection sign, and an agreed ticket format listing item, quantity and any requested variation. No customer names or advance information are needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the aggregate hourly counts to choose broadly comparable peak periods. Observe one 90-minute period with the present single line and one with the relay; repeat in reversed order if feasible. Using an existing clock, staff record join and completed-handoff times for every fifth arriving customer on anonymous tickets, with identical sampling in both conditions. Tally orders, incorrect items or quantities, corrections caught before handoff, and remakes. Record the packing backlog periodically. Reject or revise the relay if total waiting fails to improve, long waits become worse, or errors rise. A faster counter with unchanged collection times falsifies the claimed benefit. Small samples cannot establish equal error risk; any increase warrants inspection before extending the trial.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make orders ready before customers reach the counter
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the present single line and normal staff responsibilities, but move customer choice and order clarification into otherwise idle queue time. Put a short paper menu and order-slip instructions at the queue entrance, using the bakery's actual item names and current prices. Customers may write item quantities and mark any variation, then hand the slip to the staff member when their turn arrives. Verbal ordering remains available. Staff repeat the order once, confirm availability and price, and use the same slip while packing.

The mechanism is reducing counter time spent deciding, repeating names and reconstructing an order from memory. It could also reduce mistakes by giving packing a persistent written reference. It does not depend on extra staff, advance ordering, customer identification or a separate payment channel. Customers still receive service in arrival order.

This assumes a meaningful share of current counter time involves choice or clarification, and that customers can see the menu while waiting. It will help little if packing or payment already consumes nearly all service time. Poor handwriting, stale availability information and complicated forms could make service slower. Keep the slip optional and simple: item, quantity, variation. Cross out unavailable items on the sign as staff learn about them; confirm stock at the counter before taking payment. Implementation requires only paper signs and slips, plus a usable writing implement already available. If that is unavailable, test the menu and a verbal 'please choose while waiting' prompt alone, with correspondingly lower expectations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare an unchanged 90-minute single-line peak with a comparable peak using the menu and optional slips, selected using the hourly counts. Sample every fifth arrival with anonymous join and handoff timestamps using an existing clock. For those orders, also record whether a slip was used and whether counter clarification was necessary. Count all fulfilled orders and order errors in both periods. Judge the intervention by the whole queue, not just slip users, who may already have simpler orders. It fails if clarification does not fall, total waiting stays unchanged, or slip misunderstandings increase errors. Repeat before drawing conclusions if traffic or order complexity differs substantially.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Prepare a small buffer of common orders before the peak
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Before the 90-minute peak, use a capped amount of existing preparation time to pack a small buffer of the bakery's simplest, frequently requested items or standard quantities. Keep the usual single line, prices and ordering choices. When an order exactly matches a prepared pack, staff retrieve it, confirm its contents with the customer and take payment normally. All other orders follow the existing process.

The mechanism is shifting repeatable packing work out of the busiest period. Unlike a faster ordering channel, it directly reduces the work that the two staff must perform during the peak. Individually labeled packs, showing item and quantity, can also reduce hurried counting. Do not assume the hourly counts identify popular products: they indicate when demand peaks, while an initial brief tally of actual orders establishes whether any repeated pack is common enough to justify preparation.

This requires products that tolerate advance packaging under the bakery's existing food-handling rules, suitable packaging already in stock, and some available staff time before the peak. If earlier preparation would displace essential work or another busy period, the option is unsuitable. Do not prepack products whose quality, temperature control or allergen handling would be compromised. Start with one eligible product and a small quantity based on observed demand. Keep different products visibly separated and use plain labels. Customers requesting variations receive a freshly assembled order. The principal limits are demand uncertainty, storage space, packaging use and leftover stock; faster peak service should not conceal excessive preparation work or waste.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First tally eligible repeated orders during a normal peak while measuring sampled join-to-handoff times and all order errors. On a comparable day, prepare a small buffer before the peak and repeat the same observations with the single line unchanged. Record preparation minutes, packs sold, leftovers, packaging used and any label or selection errors. Use an existing clock and anonymous paper tallies; no customer data are needed. Reject the approach if waiting does not improve, preparation disrupts earlier service, errors increase, or leftovers outweigh the practical benefit. A buffer that sells out immediately may justify a modest second trial, but does not by itself prove that overall waiting improved.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Bounded priority for short orders
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep both staff able to complete an entire order, but change which waiting customer is served next. Use two paper signs: ‘One product type, up to two pieces, no changes’ and ‘All other orders.’ Customers choose a waiting group and take numbered paper tickets from one shared sequence. Verbal help remains available when a customer is unsure; classification is confirmed before service begins.

Whenever a staff member becomes free, they may call the oldest short-order ticket. However, after two consecutive short-order starts while other orders are waiting, the next start must be the oldest ticket in the other group. A shared paper tally records this sequence; staff mark it before calling a customer. If either group is empty, serve the other. Customers keep their tickets until handoff, and staff retain the usual order confirmation and packing checks.

The mechanism is reducing the time small purchases spend blocked behind lengthy orders. It changes service order rather than moving packing work, collecting orders earlier, or splitting staff into specialist roles. It could reduce average waiting when order durations vary substantially, although larger orders may wait longer and total service capacity may remain unchanged.

Prerequisites are space for two clearly marked waiting groups, customers accepting the rule, and a short-order definition that actually predicts faster service. Paper signs and numbered tickets suffice, assuming an existing writing implement. Confusing eligibility, coordinating the next ticket, or disputes about fairness could erase the benefit. If most orders take similar time, retain the single line.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the hourly counts to select comparable 90-minute peaks: one with the present single line, one with bounded priority. With an existing clock, sample every fifth arrival in both conditions and record anonymous join-to-handoff times and order category. Tally all completed orders, incorrect handoffs, corrections and remakes. Compare overall waiting and waiting within each category, including the longest observed waits. Stop or revise if errors increase, overall waiting fails to improve, or larger-order waits become unacceptable. Inspect actual service durations for a small sample: if eligible orders are not appreciably faster, the proposed mechanism lacks its necessary premise. One paired trial can expose failure but cannot establish unchanged error risk.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reduce walking and searching at the counter
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the present single line and both staff’s normal responsibilities, but rearrange existing counter materials before the peak so that routine orders require fewer trips, reaches and searches. Put commonly used empty bags and paper within reach of each existing packing position, give each utensil a fixed location, and clear a separate spot for checking and handing over completed orders. Move supplies only where existing space and food-handling rules permit. Leave products unpacked until ordered and retain the usual order confirmation and contents check.

The mechanism is reducing physical work per order. If staff repeatedly leave the counter for bags, search for utensils or wait for access to a shared surface, removing those delays releases capacity throughout the 90-minute peak without speeding up accuracy-sensitive steps. This differs from preparing orders ahead: the preparation concerns the workspace, and every purchase is still assembled on demand.

First inspect several ordinary orders and mark repeated movements on a paper sketch. Change only the most frequent avoidable movement or obstruction. Use existing supplies and paper location labels; do not buy equipment or assume duplicate utensils are available. Position enough existing empty packaging for the peak if space allows, using the aggregate hourly counts only as a rough guide to volume.

This requires a material amount of avoidable movement and a layout that can safely improve. It offers little benefit if customer decisions, payment processing or necessary packing already dominate service time. Crowding the counter or making staff cross paths could make it worse.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a normal 90-minute single-line peak with a broadly comparable peak using the revised layout. Using an existing clock and anonymous paper tallies, record join-to-handoff time for every fifth customer and count completed orders, order errors and corrections in both conditions. For a smaller sample, count supply trips, searches and staff obstruction pauses. Keep recording equally light in both periods. Reject the layout if movement does not fall, total waiting does not improve, or errors increase. Different demand or order complexity makes a single comparison inconclusive; repeat before adopting it permanently.

EXPAND.title: Give short orders limited priority within one queue
EXPAND.proposal:
Keep one physical line, but test a bounded service rule: after two ordinary orders, staff may invite the earliest customer buying just one item with no customization to the next available service position. If nobody qualifies, serve the next customer normally. Both staff continue taking, packing and charging for complete orders using their usual checks. A paper sign explains the rule; customers declare eligibility verbally when invited.

The mechanism is serving occasional short jobs earlier, which can reduce average waiting when service times vary substantially. It does not increase packing capacity, and customers with larger orders may wait longer. The two ordinary orders between invitations limit overtaking, although they do not guarantee a maximum wait. Stop making invitations whenever the oldest waiting customer would otherwise be delayed repeatedly.

This assumes single-item purchases are common and reliably quicker to complete. A single item requiring lengthy preparation or discussion does not qualify. If most transactions take similar time, priority offers little benefit and the invitation itself could slow service. It also requires a queue arrangement where a customer can approach safely without crowding others.

Implementation needs one sign and a paper tally to track the two ordinary completions between invitations. No dedicated express employee, second payment facility, customer identification or advance information is required. Staff confirm the requested item and payment in the normal way; eligibility never justifies skipping an accuracy check. This is suitable only if the bakery accepts the explicit tradeoff between average waiting and arrival-order fairness.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one ordinary 90-minute single-line peak with a broadly comparable priority trial, using hourly counts to select periods. With an existing clock, record anonymous join-to-correct-handoff times for every fifth arrival in both conditions, including item count and whether anyone overtook them. Tally completed orders, errors, corrections and complaints throughout. Inspect average waiting, the longest sampled waits, and waits for larger orders separately. Reject the rule if average waiting does not improve, larger-order waits worsen unacceptably, or errors increase. Sparse error observations cannot establish unchanged risk; repeat promising results before adoption.

EXPAND.title: Remove repeated walking and searching at the counter
EXPAND.proposal:
Keep the current single line and complete-order service, but rearrange the existing counter workspace before the peak so each order requires fewer reaches, searches and crossings. During a normal peak, make a simple paper tally of repeated movements: fetching bags, locating serving tools, finding stock and moving between packing and payment. Change only the most frequent avoidable movement in the first trial.

The mechanism is reducing physical work per order. Unlike preparing orders early or changing staff roles, this leaves production timing and responsibility unchanged. For example, if both staff repeatedly walk to a distant supply of bags, move an existing small stack within easy reach of their normal packing positions. If searching among similar products is the problem, use large paper location labels and consistent positions rather than relying on memory under pressure.

This assumes avoidable movement or searching occupies a meaningful part of service time and that supplies or labels can be repositioned safely. Benefits may be negligible if payment or customer decisions dominate. A tighter arrangement can also create interference between staff, so assess their working paths together. Preserve established food handling, allergen separation, clear exits and access to payment equipment. Do not duplicate equipment or assume additional storage is available.

Implementation requires paper labels, existing supplies and a short setup period outside the peak that does not displace essential work. Both staff walk through several typical orders before opening the changed layout. Keep a simple sketch of the original arrangement so an unsuccessful change is easy to reverse.
EXPAND.experiment: Measure a normal 90-minute single-line peak, then a comparable peak with the single layout change. Use identical anonymous every-fifth-arrival join and correct-handoff timing, an existing clock, and aggregate counts of fulfilled orders and errors. For sampled orders, also tally the targeted walk or search. The mechanism is unsupported if that movement does not decline; the service goal fails if movement declines but overall waiting does not improve. Revert if selection mistakes, staff interference or other errors increase. Demand and order mix may explain differences between days, so repeat a promising comparison before making the arrangement permanent.

EXPAND.title: Invite flexible customers to visit during a quieter window
EXPAND.proposal:
Use the week's aggregate hourly counts to identify a consistently less busy period adjacent to the 90-minute peak. Place a paper sign where existing customers can see it on earlier visits: 'If your timing is flexible, this period has usually been quieter.' Give the actual observed hours, describe the information as historical, and make no promise about future waiting or stock.

The mechanism is shifting some arrivals away from the busiest interval. Even a modest reduction in arrivals can reduce waiting when demand is close to the two staff members' service capacity. Counter service, packing checks, prices and the single line remain unchanged. Customers can still arrive whenever they choose, and no reservation, application, contact detail or purchase history is collected.

This assumes some customers are repeat visitors who see the sign before their next trip and can change their timing. It is unlikely to help a peak driven almost entirely by fixed work breaks, school schedules or one-time visitors. Hourly counts establish only relative traffic; they do not establish shorter waits, comparable staffing or product availability. Choose a suggested window only if the bakery can normally provide its existing service then without adding staff. Avoid directing demand into another already constrained period.

Implementation requires a handwritten sign and the supplied hourly counts. Leave the sign visible for several days so repeat customers have an opportunity to respond. Do not ask peak customers to leave and return: the intervention concerns voluntary future timing. The main uncertainty is whether enough customers will notice and act on the information; a small bakery may have too little timing flexibility for this to matter.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare matched weekdays before and after displaying the sign, retaining the present single line throughout. Use the supplied counts as initial context, then tally arrivals and completions during both the peak and suggested window. Sample anonymous join-to-correct-handoff times identically in both windows and count order errors. The smallest useful check needs several days of exposure, not one immediate trial. Reject or revise the sign if peak arrivals and waiting do not fall, the suggested window develops comparable congestion, or errors rise. Check combined-period completions for possible lost business. Weather, stock and normal daily variation limit causal conclusions from a short comparison.

EXPAND.title: Let customers select already wrapped items while waiting
EXPAND.proposal:
For products already individually wrapped and suitable for customer handling, let customers select their own items from an accessible display before reaching payment. Keep one checkout line and normal staff service for everything else. At the counter, customers present every selected item; staff verify product identity, quantity and price, confirm any staff-retrieved items, and take payment. Customers who prefer assistance receive it normally.

The mechanism is transferring a limited amount of retrieval work to customers and allowing that work to happen while staff serve preceding customers. It could reduce the staff time each eligible transaction requires without shortening the final accuracy check. Unlike building a buffer of prepared orders, this uses products already wrapped for ordinary sale and lets customers assemble their own selection.

This requires an existing customer-accessible display, enough space for selection without blocking the queue, and products whose wrappers and labels support reliable identification. These conditions are not established by the supplied materials. If customers would need access behind the counter, new fixtures, loose-food utensils or additional packaging work, this alternative is unsuitable within the stated resources. Aggregate hourly counts cannot establish how many purchases qualify.

Use a paper sign to identify one eligible display section and explain that all items must be presented at checkout. Keep prices visible and preserve existing food-handling and allergen information. Do not extend the trial to loose products or visually indistinguishable wrapped items. The main limits are customer congestion, handling damage, additional stock-checking work and orders that still require substantial staff retrieval.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one ordinary 90-minute peak with one trial peak on a comparable weekday, using hourly counts to help select similar demand periods. With existing timekeeping, systematically sample customers at the same interval in both sessions and record joining-to-correct-handover time on anonymous numbered tickets. Both staff tally all order errors and corrections, including wrong selections caught at checkout. Also tally completed orders and selection-related interruptions. Stop if the display obstructs the line. Reject the mechanism if total waiting fails to fall, errors increase, or retrieval savings are consumed by verification and congestion. A single pair is only a screening test; repeat before adopting if arrival volumes differ materially or errors are too rare to assess.
